To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ARV therapy for HIV/AIDS could prevent 10-30% of TB cases in the next few years and could enhance TB treatment, but that TB control programs are a crucial entry point for the delivery of ARV treatment to HIV-infected persons.

ARV drugs can prevent TB, but early therapy, plus coverage and compliance, are necessary to avert a fraction of TB cases; ARV drugs could be used to enhance TB therapy; TB programs provide an entry point for HIV treatment.

(1) ARV drugs could prevent TB in HIV-infected individuals and (2) ARV drugs, in addition to their direct effect on TB, can improve the outcome of TB treatment by enhancing adherence to therapy, reducing the emergence of drug resistance, and improving the immune response to TB.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the epidemiology, clinical features, and management of HIV/TB coinfection, with the ultimate goal of reducing the burden of TB in HIV-infected populations and preventing the spread of TB to the general population.
the impact of HIV/AIDS on tuberculosis and with the use of antiretroviral drugs for tuberculosis control.

the following: (1) understanding the role of ARV drugs in the prevention and treatment of TB in HIV-infected individuals; (2) developing new approaches to the treatment of TB in the era of HIV/AIDS; and (3) developing new approaches for the control of TB and HIV in the developing world.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ARV drugs can prevent TB in patients with HIV, but the magnitude of the effect depends on the timing and intensity of ARV therapy.
TB control is an essential element in the fight against HIV/AIDS, and that the treatment of TB in HIV-coinfected patients is a major challenge for the control of TB.
ARV drugs are an important tool for the control of TB and HIV/AIDS, and the TB program should be used as an entry point for the control of HIV/AIDS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of ARV drugs and TB drugs is synergistic and should be used to treat both HIV and TB.
the ARV drugs have the potential to prevent and treat TB and to treat HIV/AIDS.
TB control programs are an important entry point to the control of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Africa.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TB programs must integrate the treatment of HIV and that ARV drugs must be integrated with TB drugs.
TB control and HIV/AIDS treatment programs should work together to provide ARV drugs to TB patients.
ARV drugs are essential to the control of HIV/AIDS.
